newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour says its planned windfall tax is legal.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour says its planned windfall tax is legal.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party said on Thursday it had won legal assurances that its proposed tax on the profits of privatised utilities cannot be challenged in the courts.
Labour said it intended to bring in such a tax as soon as it won power, with an election due by May 22.
It would use the money to pay for a three billion pound ($4.9 billion) plan to get the long-term jobless back to work.

"We want to move quickly on this. It will be in a first budget, the budget will come within a few weeks of the general election if we are successful in persuading the country to vote for us. That budget will introduce the windfall tax," Labour's economics spokesman Gordon Brown said on BBC radio.
"We now know from our legal advice that there will be no obstacle to our doing it both quickly and to avoiding any challenge in the courts," Brown said.

Prime Minister John Major has seized on media reports that Labour's proposed windfall tax could face a challenge from the companies affected in British and European courts, and has challenged Brown to prove his plans were legal.
With Brown committed to leaving income tax rates and spending plans unchanged, the windfall tax is the centrepiece of Labour's first proposed budget, which could be announced by June.
It is the only revenue-raising commitment Brown has made, and is crucial to Labour's vow to make a difference after 18 years of Conservative rule.

But Brown refused on Thursday to detail exactly how much the tax would raise overall. He also refused to be drawn on whether the tax would cover companies such as British Airways and British Telecommunications, as well as utilities such as British Gas.
Labour sources have suggested in the past that the tax could raise five billion to 10 billion pounds.
Brown's remarks came just hours before a speech in which he will detail how he plans to use the proceeds of the tax to cut youth unemployment and get the long-term jobless back to work.
Before the speech Labour also issued an eight-page legal opinion, or report, by top lawyer and judge Michael Beloff dismissing the threat of a legal challenge to the tax.
"In our view...the windfall tax could not even attract a challenge under domestic law (and it) should not attract a challenge under EC law," Beloff said in his report.
"But, if it did, such a challenge would fail (and the tax) would withstand any challenge which may be made under the European Court of Human Rights." ($1=.6120 Pound)
